instruction: Inspect an archive's contents before extracting it.
context: tar: -t lists rather than extracts and -v adds permissions, owner, and size. Listing first reveals whether members use absolute paths or a leading directory, which decides if extraction is safe.

instruction: Pull one file out of a large archive.
context: tar: naming members after the archive extracts only those, and the path must match the listing exactly, including any leading directory. --wildcards allows a glob instead.

instruction: Extract an archive somewhere other than the current directory.
context: tar -C changes directory before acting, which is safer than cd first because it applies to that invocation only. The target directory must already exist.

instruction: Create a zstd-compressed archive for a fast backup.
context: tar: --zstd selects zstd, alongside -z for gzip, -j for bzip2, and -J for xz. zstd compresses far faster than xz at comparable ratios, which suits frequent backups.

instruction: Let tar pick the compression from the filename.
context: tar -a infers the compressor from the output extension, so the format changes with the filename alone. On extraction GNU tar detects the format automatically and -z is not required.

instruction: Extract a system backup keeping original ownership and modes.
context: tar: -p preserves permissions and --same-owner restores the recorded uid and gid, both of which require root. Extracting as an ordinary user silently remaps everything to that user.

instruction: Check a compressed archive is not corrupt without extracting it.
context: gzip -t tests integrity by decompressing to nothing and checking the stored CRC. It reports nothing on success, so a silent exit means the archive is intact.

instruction: Compress a file without removing the original.
context: gzip: -k keeps the input, which gzip otherwise deletes on success. -9 is maximum compression and -1 the fastest, with the default at -6.

instruction: Search rotated log archives without decompressing them to disk.
context: The z-prefixed tools decompress on the fly: zgrep, zcat, zless, and zdiff. They accept the same flags as the underlying command, so -i and -c behave identically.

instruction: Create a zip of a directory excluding version control files.
context: zip: -r recurses and -x excludes patterns, which must be quoted so the shell does not expand them first. The exclude pattern is matched against the stored path, not the filesystem path.

instruction: See what a zip contains before unpacking it.
context: unzip: -l lists entries with sizes and dates, and -v adds compression ratios and CRCs. -t tests every entry's checksum without writing anything.

instruction: Unpack a zip into a subdirectory to avoid scattering files.
context: unzip: -d names the destination and creates it if missing, unlike tar -C which requires it to exist. -q suppresses the per-file listing and -o overwrites without prompting.

instruction: Compress a large dataset using all CPU cores.
context: zstd: -T0 uses every available core, the level runs from 1 to 19, and --long widens the match window for large redundant files. --ultra unlocks levels above 19.

instruction: Decompress an xz file while keeping the compressed copy.
context: xz: -d decompresses, -k keeps the input, and -T0 threads the work. xz achieves high ratios but is markedly slower than zstd, which matters for anything compressed routinely.

instruction: Encode a binary file as a single line of base64.
context: base64: GNU wraps output at 76 columns by default, and -w 0 disables wrapping, which matters when embedding in JSON or a header. BSD base64 does not wrap and has no -w.

instruction: Decode a base64 payload back to a file.
context: base64: GNU spells decode -d and BSD spells it -D, a case difference that breaks portable scripts. -i ignores non-alphabet characters such as embedded newlines.

instruction: Inspect the first bytes of a file to identify its format.
context: hexdump -C is canonical mode, showing hex alongside ASCII, and -n limits the byte count. xxd produces similar output and can reverse it with -r, which hexdump cannot.

instruction: Rebuild a binary file from a hex dump.
context: xxd: -r reverses a dump back to binary and -p means the plain continuous hex format with no offsets or ASCII column. Both flags must match how the dump was produced.

instruction: Find readable text embedded in a binary.
context: strings: -n sets the minimum run length, filtering the noise that the default of four produces. -t d prints the decimal byte offset of each match, which locates it for patching.

instruction: Unpack an initramfs image.
context: cpio: -i extracts, -d creates directories, -m preserves modification times, and -v lists members. It reads the archive from standard input rather than taking a filename.

instruction: Unpack a Debian package to inspect its contents.
context: A .deb is an ar archive containing debian-binary plus two tarballs, control and data. ar x extracts them, after which the data tarball holds the installed files.

instruction: Produce a checksum manifest for every file in a tree.
context: Batching with -exec + keeps the invocation count low, and the manifest format is exactly what sha256sum -c consumes later. Sort the output for a reproducible manifest.

instruction: Find the first byte at which two binary files differ.
context: cmp reports the byte and line of the first difference, and -l lists every differing byte in octal. It is far cheaper than diff for binaries because it stops at the first mismatch by default.

instruction: Select array elements matching a condition and print one field.
context: jq: .items[] streams array elements, select keeps those where the expression is true, and the pipe chains filters. -r strips the quotes from string output.

instruction: Extract a string value for use in a shell variable.
context: jq -r prints strings without surrounding quotes and without escaping, which is what shell consumers need. Without it the value arrives wrapped in literal quote characters.

instruction: Flatten JSON records into tab-separated columns.
context: jq: the @tsv and @csv filters take an array and emit a correctly escaped row, handling embedded tabs and quotes. -r is required or the whole row arrives as one quoted string.

instruction: Discover the structure of an unfamiliar JSON document.
context: jq: keys lists an object's field names sorted, and keys_unsorted preserves document order. paths gives every nested location, which maps a deep document quickly.

instruction: Read a field that may be absent without failing.
context: jq: the // operator supplies an alternative when the left side is null or false, which covers a missing key. Note it also fires on a legitimate false, unlike a pure existence check.

instruction: Aggregate a JSON Lines file into a single array.
context: jq -s slurps every input value into one array, which is how to run array-wide filters like length or group_by over JSON Lines. Without it each line is processed independently.

instruction: Count JSON records grouped by a field value.
context: jq: group_by requires sorted input and returns an array of arrays, so map reduces each group. The trailing @tsv converts the objects into printable rows.

instruction: Reformat pretty-printed JSON into one line per record.
context: jq -c emits each result on a single line, which is exactly the JSON Lines format. The inverse, pretty-printing a compact file, is the default with no flag at all.

instruction: Update a value in a JSON config from the shell.
context: jq: --arg binds a shell string to a jq variable safely, avoiding the quoting break that string interpolation causes. --argjson does the same for a JSON value such as a number or object.

instruction: Read a nested value out of a YAML file.
context: yq applies jq-style expressions to YAML, so path syntax and -r carry over directly. -o json converts the document to JSON for tools that cannot read YAML.

instruction: Select named columns from a CSV that has quoted fields containing commas.
context: csvcut understands RFC 4180 quoting, so a comma inside a quoted field does not split a column the way cut -d, would. -n lists the column names and their indexes first.

instruction: Encode a secret in the format authenticator apps expect.
context: base32 uses a case-insensitive alphabet with no easily confused characters, which is why TOTP seeds use it rather than base64. -d decodes and -w controls line wrapping as with base64.

instruction: Archive exactly the files named in a list.
context: tar -T reads member paths from a file, one per line, which sidesteps command-line length limits. --null combined with -T reads NUL-separated paths from find -print0.

instruction: Break a large archive into pieces small enough to upload.
context: split -b takes a size with a unit suffix and appends generated suffixes to the given prefix. Reassembly is just cat of the parts in sorted order, so the prefix should sort correctly.

instruction: Encrypt a backup with a passphrase rather than a key pair.
context: gpg -c uses symmetric encryption with a passphrase and no keyring, writing a .gpg file. --cipher-algo overrides the compiled-in default, which on older builds is weaker than AES256.

instruction: Decode base64 on macOS.
context: BSD base64 spells decode with a capital -D where GNU uses lowercase -d, and takes its input file with -i rather than positionally. This is a frequent cause of scripts failing on macOS only.

instruction: Extract one member from an archive on macOS.
context: macOS tar is bsdtar from libarchive, which accepts the common GNU flags including -C and --strip-components. It lacks --wildcards, treating member patterns as globs by default instead.

instruction: Extract readable text from a Mach-O binary.
context: BSD strings needs a lone dash to scan the whole file rather than only the initialized data sections, which is the opposite of the GNU default. -t d for offsets works the same.

instruction: Compute a SHA-256 checksum on macOS.
context: macOS has no sha256sum; shasum -a selects the algorithm and its output format matches, so shasum -a 256 -c reads a GNU-generated manifest. The bare sha256 command exists too but formats differently.
